title: Al-Maajid, the Noble
tomorrow: Al-Wahid, the One. one what, exactly?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Wajid, the Finder: the found are rich in soul, and become finders. The line: lacking nothing. And a question about two hands.

Splitting the check. One friend always reaches for it first; another always seems to have forgotten a wallet. Without saying so, people keep score of who gives. The Prophet, peace be upon him, settled the question of the two hands in one line: the upper hand is better than the lower hand. The upper hand is the one that gives; the lower is the one that asks. Today's Name puts that in God's own terms. Al-Maajid, the Noble, glorious in generosity.
screen: `WHO REACHES FOR THE CHECK?` → `THE UPPER HAND GIVES.` → `GLORIOUS IN GENEROSITY.`

segments.voice: One question today: what makes someone noble? In the Qur'an, glory shows up as a gift. Angels bring Abraham's household news of a son in old age, his wife laughs, and they answer, in Pickthall's words: "Lo! He is Owner of Praise, Owner of Glory!" God's glory, in that scene, is generosity to an old couple. So for people, noble isn't a title or a family name. It's the upper hand. And the same hadith adds two practical lines: begin with those you're responsible for, and the best charity comes from what's beyond your own needs. Here's where a neighbor tradition sounds very close. In the Bible's book of Acts, Paul tells a group of church elders to remember "the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to give than to receive." Shared, then: the giving hand is the honored one. A church meal train and a Muslim's sadaqa look alike from across the table. And one honest difference. In Islam, one kind of giving, zakat, is a pillar, a duty with its own rules, named in the hadith that says Islam is built on five. Churches each have their own ways with giving, and the line in Acts speaks of blessing, not a fixed share. Two traditions, each in its own words. The giving hand is noble in both.
screen: `GLORY SHOWS UP AS A GIFT.` · `THE UPPER HAND, BEGINNING AT HOME.` · `MORE BLESSED TO GIVE.` · `ZAKAT: A PILLAR WITH RULES.` · then, large: `NOBLE.`

segments.voice: Choose one act only the upper hand can do: pay for someone's coffee, give credit out loud to the person who earned it, hand over the last slice. Plan it now in detail: who, when, how. Then sit with the plan for the two minutes, quietly, since noble doesn't need an audience.
Al-Maajid. The Noble: glory that shows itself by giving, Owner of Praise, Owner of Glory.
The one to keep: noble, the hand that gives without keeping any score. Good night.

howItsDone: Muslims give zakat, a required share of wealth, and sadaqa, charity given freely, beginning with family and those in need nearby; Al-Maajid is called on among the Names.

fork.setup: you win $100 in a school contest. your little brother needs new cleats, and a classmate is raising money for a shelter. what does the 'upper hand' hadith say to do first?
options: give it all to the shelter; strangers count most.
start with the one you're responsible for, then give from what's left over.
keep it; you earned it, and charity is for adults.
fork.reveal: the hadith that praises the upper hand also says: begin with your dependents, and the best charity is from what's beyond your needs. cleats first, then the shelter.

original.note: Arabic: the Noble, glorious in generosity. a close form, majid, 'Owner of Glory', is in Surah Hud.

what a scholar hears: al-Maajid in the traditional list; hamidun majid in 11:73; the upper hand (Sahih al-Bukhari 1427–1429); Acts 20:35 as a neighbor's saying.

chat.says: jordan's grandma's church has brought dinner 6 nights. dadi wants to pay them back. grandma said no. now?
options: Don't pay. Give onward: Dadi could cook for their next family in need.
Pay anyway. Taking without paying keeps Dadi the lower hand.
Nothing. It's their religion's thing, so it isn't ours to return.
chat.meaning: The upper hand gives, and Acts calls giving more blessed. Paying would undo their gift; giving onward keeps it moving.
